C7.2 Coupled Oscillators - Simple Case#

C7.2.1 Motivation#

Many physical systems are composed of parts that influence each other’s motion. A violin string vibrates because each tiny element of the string pulls on its neighbors. In molecules, atoms are connected by chemical bonds that transmit vibrations between them. Buildings, bridges, and even the human body contain interconnected parts whose motions are not independent.

When two or more oscillators are linked through a physical connection — a spring, a rod, a field, or even an electrical circuit — we call the system coupled. Such coupling allows energy to be exchanged between components, leading to rich behaviors such as beats, resonance splitting, and normal modes. Understanding coupled oscillators is therefore a critical step toward understanding collective motion, wave propagation, and normal mode decomposition that appear throughout physics and engineering.

C7.2.2 Example: Two Masses Connected by Springs#

Consider the simplest case of two identical masses \(m\) connected by three springs of equal spring constant \(k\):

import numpy as np

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2))
ax.set_xlim(0, 14)
ax.set_ylim(-1, 2)
ax.axis('off')

# Function to draw a spring
def draw_spring(x_start, x_end, y=0.5, coils=8, amp=0.2):
    x = np.linspace(x_start, x_end, coils*2 + 1)
    y_spring = y + amp * ((-1)**np.arange(len(x)))
    ax.plot(x, y_spring, color='gray', linewidth=2)

# Equilibrium positions (where x1=0 and x2=0)
eq1, eq2 = 5, 11  # centers of the masses at equilibrium

# Current (displaced) positions
x1_pos = eq1 + 0.8  # displaced to the right
x2_pos = eq2 - 0.6  # displaced to the left

# Walls
ax.plot([0, 0], [0, 1], color='black', linewidth=4)
ax.plot([14, 14], [0, 1], color='black', linewidth=4)

# Springs (connected between elements)
draw_spring(0, x1_pos - 1)
draw_spring(x1_pos + 1, x2_pos - 1)
draw_spring(x2_pos + 1, 14)

# Masses
ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x1_pos - 1, 0), 2, 1, facecolor='lightblue', edgecolor='black'))
ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x2_pos - 1, 0), 2, 1, facecolor='lightblue', edgecolor='black'))

# Mass labels
ax.text(x1_pos, 0.4, r"$m_1$", fontsize=14, ha='center')
ax.text(x2_pos, 0.4, r"$m_2$", fontsize=14, ha='center')

# Equilibrium dashed lines
ax.plot([eq1, eq1], [-0.5, 1.3], 'k--', linewidth=1)
ax.plot([eq2, eq2], [-0.5, 1.3], 'k--', linewidth=1)
ax.text(eq1, 1.4, r"$x_1=0$", fontsize=11, ha='center')
ax.text(eq2, 1.4, r"$x_2=0$", fontsize=11, ha='center')

# Displacement arrows (x1, x2)
ax.arrow(eq1, -0.2, x1_pos - eq1, 0, 
         head_width=0.07, head_length=0.15, fc='r', ec='r', linewidth=1.5)
ax.arrow(eq2, -0.2, x2_pos - eq2, 0, 
         head_width=0.07, head_length=0.15, fc='r', ec='r', linewidth=1.5)

# Displacement labels
ax.text((eq1 + x1_pos)/2, -0.4, r"$x_1$", color='r', fontsize=13, ha='center')
ax.text((eq2 + x2_pos)/2, -0.4, r"$x_2$", color='r', fontsize=13, ha='center')

# Spring and wall labels
ax.text(2, 1.3, r"$k$", fontsize=12, ha='center')
ax.text(8, 1.3, r"$k$", fontsize=12, ha='center')
ax.text(13, 1.3, r"$k$", fontsize=12, ha='center')
ax.text(0, 1.3, "Wall", fontsize=12, ha='center')
ax.text(14, 1.3, "Wall", fontsize=12, ha='center')

Let \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) denote the displacements of the two masses from their equilibrium positions. The left and right walls are fixed.

The forces on the two masses follow from Hooke’s law:

\[ F_1 = -k x_1 + k (x_2 - x_1), \]
\[ F_2 = -k x_2 + k (x_1 - x_2). \]

Each mass experiences a restoring force from both its own spring to the wall and the coupling spring connecting it to the other mass.

C7.2.3 Equations of Motion#

Applying Newton’s second law to each mass gives:

\[ m\ddot{x}_1 = -2k x_1 + k x_2, \]
\[ m\ddot{x}_2 = -2k x_2 + k x_1. \]

These can be written in matrix form as:

\[\begin{split} m \begin{pmatrix} \ddot{x}_1 \\[4pt] \ddot{x}_2 \end{pmatrix} = -k \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\[4pt] -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\[4pt] x_2 \end{pmatrix}. \end{split}\]

This coupled set of differential equations shows that the acceleration of each mass depends on both displacements. To solve this, we look for normal modes — special patterns of motion where both masses oscillate with the same frequency.

C7.2.4 Normal Mode Solutions#

We assume trial solutions of the form:

\[ x_1 = A_1 \cos(\omega t), \quad x_2 = A_2 \cos(\omega t). \]

Substituting into the equations of motion gives the algebraic system:

\[\begin{split} \begin{pmatrix} 2k - m\omega^2 & -k \\[4pt] -k & 2k - m\omega^2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} A_1 \\[4pt] A_2 \end{pmatrix} = 0. \end{split}\]

Box Activity 1: From trial solutions to the algebraic system

You have the coupled equations of motion

\[ m\ddot{x}_1 = -2k\,x_1 + k\,x_2, \qquad m\ddot{x}_2 = -2k\,x_2 + k\,x_1. \]

Assume normal-mode trial solutions with a common angular frequency \(\omega\):

\[ x_1(t)=A_1\cos(\omega t), \qquad x_2(t)=A_2\cos(\omega t). \]

Your task: Show that these lead to the algebraic (matrix) system for \((A_1,A_2)\):

\[\begin{split} \begin{pmatrix} 2k - m\omega^2 & -k \\[4pt] -k & 2k - m\omega^2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} A_1 \\[2pt] A_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\[2pt] 0 \end{pmatrix}. \end{split}\]

Work it out explicitly:

  1. Compute the second derivatives:

\[ \ddot{x}_1(t)=\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_, \qquad \ddot{x}_2(t)=\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_. \]

  1. Substitute \(x_1,x_2,\ddot{x}_1,\ddot{x}_2\) into the equations of motion and factor out \(\cos(\omega t)\):

\[ m\ddot{x}_1 + 2k\,x_1 - k\,x_2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; (\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_)A_1 + (\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_)A_2 = 0, \]
\[ m\ddot{x}_2 + 2k\,x_2 - k\,x_1 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; (\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_)A_2 + (\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_)A_1 = 0. \]

  1. Arrange your two linear equations in matrix form and verify it matches the target system above.

Hint (click to expand)
Use $\ddot{x}_j(t) = -\omega^2 A_j \cos(\omega t)$ and cancel the common $\cos(\omega t)\neq 0$.

You should arrive at

\[ (2k - m\omega^2)A_1 - kA_2 = 0,\qquad -kA_1 + (2k - m\omega^2)A_2 = 0. \]

Box Activity 2: Solving for the Normal Mode Frequencies

You have derived the algebraic system for the amplitudes:

\[\begin{split} \begin{pmatrix} 2k - m\omega^2 & -k \\[4pt] -k & 2k - m\omega^2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} A_1 \\[2pt] A_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\[2pt] 0 \end{pmatrix}. \end{split}\]

For a nontrivial solution (nonzero amplitudes), the determinant of the coefficient matrix must vanish:

\[\begin{split} \begin{vmatrix} 2k - m\omega^2 & -k \\[4pt] -k & 2k - m\omega^2 \end{vmatrix} = 0. \end{split}\]

Your task: Show that this leads to two distinct frequencies of oscillation, \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\).

Work through the following steps:

  1. Expand the determinant:

\[ (2k - m\omega^2)^2 - (\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_) = 0. \]

  1. Simplify the resulting equation to solve for \(m\omega^2\):

\[ (2k - m\omega^2) = \pm \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_. \]

  1. Solve for the two possible values of \(\omega^2\):

\[ \omega^2_1 = \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_, \qquad \omega^2_2 = \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_. \]

  1. Finally, write down the two normal mode frequencies \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\) and identify which corresponds to the symmetric and antisymmetric motion.

Hint (click to expand)

Compute the determinant:

\[ (2k - m\omega^2)^2 - k^2 = 0. \]

Simplify:

\[ 2k - m\omega^2 = \pm k. \]

Therefore,

\[ m\omega^2 = k \quad \text{or} \quad m\omega^2 = 3k. \]

So the two mode frequencies are:

\[ \boxed{\omega_1 = \sqrt{\tfrac{k}{m}}, \qquad \omega_2 = \sqrt{\tfrac{3k}{m}}.} \]

C7.2.5 Physical Meaning of the Modes#

Box Activity 3: Determining the Amplitude Ratios for Each Mode

You have found the two normal mode frequencies:

\[ \omega_1 = \sqrt{\tfrac{k}{m}}, \qquad \omega_2 = \sqrt{\tfrac{3k}{m}}. \]

Now, determine the relationship between the amplitudes \(A_1\) and \(A_2\) for each of these frequencies.
Start from one of the equations in the algebraic system:

\[ (2k - m\omega^2)A_1 - kA_2 = 0. \]

Your task: Show that

  • for the lower frequency \(\omega_1\), the two masses move in phase (\(A_1 = A_2\)),

  • for the higher frequency \(\omega_2\), the two masses move out of phase (\(A_1 = -A_2\)).

Work through the following steps:

  1. Substitute \(\omega_1^2 = \tfrac{k}{m}\) into the equation and simplify:

\[ (2k - m\tfrac{k}{m})A_1 - kA_2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; (\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_)A_1 - kA_2 = 0. \]

  1. Solve for \(\tfrac{A_1}{A_2}\) and state the relationship between \(A_1\) and \(A_2\) for \(\omega_1\).

  2. Repeat for \(\omega_2^2 = \tfrac{3k}{m}\):

\[ (2k - m\tfrac{3k}{m})A_1 - kA_2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; (\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_)A_1 - kA_2 = 0. \]

  1. Solve for \(\tfrac{A_1}{A_2}\) and describe the motion.

Hint (click to expand)

For \(\omega_1^2 = k/m\):

\[ (2k - k)A_1 - kA_2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; k(A_1 - A_2) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; A_1 = A_2. \]

For \(\omega_2^2 = 3k/m\):

\[ (2k - 3k)A_1 - kA_2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; -k(A_1 + A_2) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; A_1 = -A_2. \]

Thus:

\[\begin{split} \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \text{Lower frequency } (\omega_1): &\quad A_1 = A_2 \quad \text{(in-phase)} \\[4pt] \text{Higher frequency } (\omega_2): &\quad A_1 = -A_2 \quad \text{(out-of-phase)} \end{aligned} } \end{split}\]

  1. Symmetric Mode (Lower Frequency)
    For \(\omega_1 = \sqrt{k/m}\), both masses move in phase with equal amplitude (\(A_1 = A_2\)).
    The coupling spring does not stretch, so only the outer springs contribute to the restoring force.
    The system behaves as if each mass were attached to its own spring — a gentle, slow oscillation.

  2. Antisymmetric Mode (Higher Frequency)
    For \(\omega_2 = \sqrt{3k/m}\), the masses move out of phase (\(A_1 = -A_2\)).
    The middle spring is alternately stretched and compressed, adding extra restoring force.
    The result is a stiffer effective system and hence a higher frequency.

C7.2.6 General Motion and Energy Exchange#

Any arbitrary motion of the two masses can be expressed as a superposition of these two normal modes:

\[ x_1(t) = C_1 \cos(\omega_1 t) + C_2 \cos(\omega_2 t), \]
\[ x_2(t) = C_1 \cos(\omega_1 t) - C_2 \cos(\omega_2 t). \]

If only one mass is displaced initially, energy will periodically transfer back and forth between the two — producing beats. This exchange reflects the interference between the two normal mode frequencies.

C7.2.7 Example#

Beats and energy exchange in the two–mass system

Setup For the symmetric three–spring system (all springs of constant \(k\) and masses \(m\)), the normal mode frequencies are

\[ \omega_1=\sqrt{\tfrac{k}{m}},\qquad \omega_2=\sqrt{\tfrac{3k}{m}}, \]

with mode shapes \([1,\,1]^T\) (in–phase) and \([1,\,-1]^T\) (out–of–phase), respectively.

A general motion can be written as

\[ x_1(t)=C_1\cos(\omega_1 t)+C_2\cos(\omega_2 t),\qquad x_2(t)=C_1\cos(\omega_1 t)-C_2\cos(\omega_2 t). \]

Initial condition that produces beats Take a simple “localized kick” (that is, only one mass is displaced):

\[ x_1(0)=X_0,\quad x_2(0)=0,\qquad \dot x_1(0)=\dot x_2(0)=0. \]

From \(t=0\),

\[ x_1(0)=C_1+C_2=X_0,\qquad x_2(0)=C_1-C_2=0 \;\Rightarrow\; C_1=C_2=\frac{X_0}{2}. \]

Thus

\[ x_1(t)=\frac{X_0}{2}\big[\cos(\omega_1 t)+\cos(\omega_2 t)\big],\qquad x_2(t)=\frac{X_0}{2}\big[\cos(\omega_1 t)-\cos(\omega_2 t)\big]. \]

Sum–to–product and the beat envelope Define the mean and difference frequencies

\[ \bar\omega=\frac{\omega_1+\omega_2}{2},\qquad \Delta\omega=\omega_2-\omega_1>0. \]

Use the identity \(\cos a\pm \cos b=2\cos\!\big(\tfrac{a\pm b}{2}\big)\cos\!\big(\tfrac{a\mp b}{2}\big)\):

\[ x_1(t)=X_0\,\cos(\bar\omega t)\,\cos\!\Big(\frac{\Delta\omega\, t}{2}\Big),\qquad x_2(t)=X_0\,\sin(\bar\omega t)\,\sin\!\Big(\frac{\Delta\omega\, t}{2}\Big). \]

Interpretation:

  • The fast oscillation occurs at \(\bar\omega\).

  • The slow envelope modulates with \(\tfrac{\Delta\omega}{2}\) via \(\cos\!\big(\tfrac{\Delta\omega t}{2}\big)\) or \(\sin\!\big(\tfrac{\Delta\omega t}{2}\big)\).

  • Successive amplitude maxima (envelope peaks) are separated by the beat period

\[ T_{\text{beat}}=\frac{2\pi}{\Delta\omega}. \]

Energy exchange between the two masses Kinetic plus potential energies (quadratic in \(x_j\) and \(\dot x_j\)) oscillate between the two masses because \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are out of phase in their envelopes:

  • When \(\cos\!\big(\tfrac{\Delta\omega t}{2}\big)\approx \pm 1\), mass 1 carries nearly all the energy while \(x_2\)’s envelope is near zero.

  • When \(\sin\!\big(\tfrac{\Delta\omega t}{2}\big)\approx \pm 1\), the situation reverses and mass 2 carries nearly all the energy.

Because energy \(\propto\) amplitude\(^2\), the energy transfer completes a full swap twice as fast as the displacement envelope:

\[ T_{\text{swap}}=\frac{\pi}{\Delta\omega},\qquad \text{(time between “all energy in } m_1\text{” and “all energy in } m_2\text{”)}. \]

Explicit envelopes From the expressions above,

\[ \text{amp}[x_1](t)=|X_0\,\cos(\tfrac{\Delta\omega t}{2})|,\qquad \text{amp}[x_2](t)=|X_0\,\sin(\tfrac{\Delta\omega t}{2})|. \]

Hence displacement beats with period \(T_{\text{beat}}=2\pi/\Delta\omega\), while energy shuttles back and forth with \(T_{\text{swap}}=\pi/\Delta\omega\).

For this specific system With \(\omega_1=\sqrt{k/m}\) and \(\omega_2=\sqrt{3k/m}\),

\[ \Delta\omega=\sqrt{\frac{3k}{m}}-\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\big(\sqrt{3}-1\big), \]

so

\[ T_{\text{beat}}=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\tfrac{k}{m}}(\sqrt{3}-1)},\qquad T_{\text{swap}}=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{\tfrac{k}{m}}(\sqrt{3}-1)}. \]

%reset -f

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# --- System parameters ---
m, k = 1.0, 1.0
X0 = 1.0

# Frequencies
omega1 = np.sqrt(k/m)
omega2 = np.sqrt(3*k/m)
delta  = omega2 - omega1

# Time range (20 seconds)
t = np.linspace(0, 20, 4000)

# Displacements
C1 = C2 = X0/2
x1 = C1*np.cos(omega1*t) + C2*np.cos(omega2*t)
x2 = C1*np.cos(omega1*t) - C2*np.cos(omega2*t)

# Envelopes (only two physical ones)
env1 = X0*np.cos(0.5*delta*t)
env2 = X0*np.sin(0.5*delta*t)

# --- Plot setup ---
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))

# Displacement curves
ax.plot(t, x1, color='tab:blue', label=r"$x_1(t)$")
ax.plot(t, x2, color='tab:orange', label=r"$x_2(t)$")

# Envelopes (distinguishable colors and styles)
ax.plot(t,  env1, linestyle="--", color='navy', alpha=0.6, label=r"Envelope of $x_1$")
ax.plot(t, -env1, linestyle="--", color='navy', alpha=0.6)
ax.plot(t,  env2, linestyle=":", color='darkorange', alpha=0.6, label=r"Envelope of $x_2$")
ax.plot(t, -env2, linestyle=":", color='darkorange', alpha=0.6)

# Axis labels and title
ax.set_xlabel("time [s]")
ax.set_ylabel("displacement [a.u.]")
ax.set_title("Beats in a Two-Mass System (Energy Exchange)")

# Legend
ax.legend(ncol=2, loc="upper right", fontsize=10)

# Grid and layout
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML, display

# ensure JS-based display for animations
plt.rcParams['animation.html'] = 'jshtml'

# --- system parameters ---
m, k = 1.0, 1.0
X0 = 1.0
sim_time = 20.0   # total time [s]
fps = 30          # animation frame rate

# --- frequencies ---
omega1 = np.sqrt(k/m)
omega2 = np.sqrt(3*k/m)
delta  = omega2 - omega1
print(f"ω1 = {omega1:.3f},  ω2 = {omega2:.3f},  Δω = {delta:.3f}")

# --- time array ---
t = np.linspace(0, sim_time, int(fps*sim_time))

# initial conditions: x1(0)=X0, x2(0)=0
C1 = C2 = X0/2
x1 = C1*np.cos(omega1*t) + C2*np.cos(omega2*t)
x2 = C1*np.cos(omega1*t) - C2*np.cos(omega2*t)

# --- geometry for visualization ---
Xeq1, Xeq2 = 0.0, 3.0    # equilibrium positions
mass_w, mass_h = 0.5, 0.4
scale = 0.6               # scale for visual displacement

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.5))
ax.set_xlim(-2, 5)
ax.set_ylim(-0.5, 1.5)
ax.axis("off")

# track and walls
ax.plot([-2, 5], [0, 0])
ax.plot([-2, -2], [0, 1.0], lw=4)
ax.plot([5, 5], [0, 1.0], lw=4)
ax.text(-2, 1.1, "Wall", ha="center")
ax.text(5, 1.1, "Wall", ha="center")

# masses
m1 = plt.Rectangle((Xeq1 - mass_w/2, 0), mass_w, mass_h, fc="#9ecae1", ec="black")
m2 = plt.Rectangle((Xeq2 - mass_w/2, 0), mass_w, mass_h, fc="#fdae6b", ec="black")
ax.add_patch(m1)
ax.add_patch(m2)

# labels
label_m1 = ax.text(Xeq1, 0.55, r"$m_1$", ha="center", fontsize=12)
label_m2 = ax.text(Xeq2, 0.55, r"$m_2$", ha="center", fontsize=12)
time_txt = ax.text(0.02, 0.9, "", transform=ax.transAxes)

# --- animation functions ---
def init():
    m1.set_xy((Xeq1 - mass_w/2, 0))
    m2.set_xy((Xeq2 - mass_w/2, 0))
    label_m1.set_x(Xeq1)
    label_m2.set_x(Xeq2)
    time_txt.set_text("")
    return m1, m2, label_m1, label_m2, time_txt

def update(frame):
    x1_now = scale * x1[frame]
    x2_now = scale * x2[frame]
    m1.set_x(Xeq1 + x1_now - mass_w/2)
    m2.set_x(Xeq2 + x2_now - mass_w/2)
    label_m1.set_x(Xeq1 + x1_now)
    label_m2.set_x(Xeq2 + x2_now)
    time_txt.set_text(f"t = {t[frame]:.2f} s")
    return m1, m2, label_m1, label_m2, time_txt

anim = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=len(t), init_func=init, interval=1000/fps, blit=True)

# display inline
display(HTML(anim.to_jshtml()))

ω1 = 1.000,  ω2 = 1.732,  Δω = 0.732

C7.2.8 Broader Perspective#

Coupled oscillators reveal a fundamental organizing principle in physics: complex motion can be decomposed into independent normal modes. Each mode oscillates with its own characteristic frequency and shape, unaffected by the others.

This principle extends far beyond two masses and springs:

  • Vibrations of molecules correspond to normal modes of atomic motion.

  • Vibrating strings and membranes can be understood as infinite sets of coupled oscillators — leading directly to wave equations.

  • Electrical circuits, optical cavities, and even quantum fields are governed by similar coupled-mode structures.

By mastering the analysis of coupled oscillators, we gain a universal tool for understanding how individual elements interact to produce collective dynamics.
